title: The Bible
author: Multiple authors; Christian scriptural traditions
summary: A collection of narrative, law, poetry, prophecy, Gospels, and letters. Read each genre on its own terms, with attention to its historical and religious setting.
context: Christian traditions receive different biblical canons. The Old Testament overlaps with Jewish scripture, but its arrangement and interpretation are not interchangeable with Jewish readings.
editionNote: Choose a named translation with notes. Catholic, Protestant, and Orthodox editions differ in their contents; compare translations before building an argument around a single English word.

readingPath.title: Mark
readingPath.note: Begin with a complete Gospel to follow its narrative.

readingPath.title: Psalms and Ecclesiastes
readingPath.note: Compare prayer, lament, and wisdom as different forms of attention.

readingPath.title: Genesis and Exodus
readingPath.note: Return to the larger narrative of creation, covenant, and liberation.

keyInsights: Literary genre changes how a passage should be read.
Read individual verses within the argument or narrative around them.
Interpretive disagreements are part of the history of biblical reading.

title: The Tanakh
author: Multiple authors; Jewish scriptural tradition
summary: The Jewish Bible comprises Torah, Nevi’im (Prophets), and Ketuvim (Writings). Reading alongside commentary reveals a continuing tradition of argument and interpretation.
context: Torah names the first five books in this context. It is not another name for the whole Tanakh. Jewish interpretation should remain visible in a cross-tradition library.
editionNote: Sefaria places Hebrew texts alongside named translations and commentaries. Check the selected version and distinguish the biblical passage from later interpretation.

readingPath.title: Genesis
readingPath.note: Read the family narratives with an accompanying commentary.

readingPath.title: Exodus
readingPath.note: Follow liberation, covenant, and communal responsibility.

readingPath.title: Psalms and Job
readingPath.note: Compare praise and protest without forcing them into one voice.

keyInsights: A collection contains multiple genres and historical voices.
Commentary can preserve disagreement rather than eliminate it.
Torah, Prophets, and Writings form distinct divisions.

title: The Quran
author: Islamic scripture
summary: The central scripture of Islam, received by Muslims as divine revelation in Arabic. Its recitation, ethical address, and theological claims belong together.
context: An English translation is an interpretation of the Arabic text. Tafsir adds a further layer of commentary; neither should silently replace the source.
editionNote: Use Quran.com with a named translation and consult tafsir for context. Record the surah and verse when citing a passage.

readingPath.title: Al-Fatihah
readingPath.note: Begin with the opening chapter and its place in prayer.

readingPath.title: Maryam and Yusuf
readingPath.note: Read sustained narratives with commentary.

readingPath.title: A guided full reading
readingPath.note: Use a study edition to follow recurring themes across surahs.

keyInsights: Arabic remains central to the text’s religious life.
Translation choices affect the reading of key concepts.
A verse’s surrounding discourse matters for interpretation.

title: The Bhagavad Gita
author: Traditionally attributed to Vyasa
summary: A dialogue between Krishna and Arjuna about action, knowledge, devotion, and liberation, situated within the Mahabharata.
context: Arjuna’s crisis is ethical and religious. Reducing the work to productivity advice strips away the devotional setting and the difficulty of his decision.
editionNote: Eknath Easwaran offers an accessible English edition. Compare a second named translation when studying philosophical terms or differences between Hindu schools.

readingPath.title: Arjuna’s crisis
readingPath.note: Read chapters 1–2 for the situation that makes the teaching necessary.

readingPath.title: Action and devotion
readingPath.note: Read chapters 3 and 12 together.

readingPath.title: The whole dialogue
readingPath.note: Return to the full work before isolating a favourite teaching.

keyInsights: The text considers several paths within a larger religious vision.
Action without attachment does not mean absence of responsibility.
Different schools interpret the relation between self and ultimate reality differently.

sources.title: Blue Mountain Center: The Bhagavad Gita

title: The Upanishads
author: Multiple teachers and textual traditions
summary: A family of texts exploring self, ultimate reality, knowledge, and liberation through dialogues, stories, and instruction.
context: The Upanishads are not one book by one author. Their interpretations shape several Vedanta traditions with substantial philosophical differences.
editionNote: Easwaran’s edition is a selection. Check its contents rather than assuming any single English volume contains every Upanishad.

readingPath.title: Katha
readingPath.note: Start with Nachiketa’s encounter with death.

readingPath.title: Isha and Kena
readingPath.note: Compare the compact forms of philosophical questioning.

readingPath.title: Chandogya and Brihadaranyaka
readingPath.note: Read longer dialogues with scholarly or traditional notes.

keyInsights: Stories and teacher-student exchanges carry philosophical work.
Atman and Brahman require contextual reading.
Later schools disagree about how the texts fit together.

title: The Dhammapada
author: Teachings attributed to the Buddha
summary: A Buddhist verse collection concerned with conduct, attention, suffering, and the path of practice.
context: The verses belong within Buddhist ethical and contemplative teaching. Reading them only as motivational sayings obscures that context.
editionNote: Choose a named translation. Easwaran’s edition includes an interpretive introduction; keep that commentary distinct from the translated verses.

readingPath.title: The opening pairs
readingPath.note: Notice the connection between intention and action.

readingPath.title: Heedfulness
readingPath.note: Read the verses as ethical instruction as well as advice about attention.

readingPath.title: A second translation
readingPath.note: Compare a small passage rather than collecting isolated quotations.

keyInsights: Attention and conduct are linked throughout the collection.
Compact verses benefit from wider Buddhist context.
A translation is a reading of the text, not a neutral copy.

title: The Heart Sutra
author: Mahayana Buddhist scripture
summary: A short Perfection of Wisdom scripture centred on emptiness and the relation between form and emptiness.
context: Emptiness is a Buddhist philosophical teaching. It should not be flattened into nihilism or treated as an early statement of quantum physics.
editionNote: 84000’s Toh 21 translation supplies source identification and notes. Other traditions transmit different versions and recitation practices.

readingPath.title: Read the complete sutra
readingPath.note: Its brevity makes reading the whole text possible before analysis.

readingPath.title: Study the notes
readingPath.note: Track terms such as form and emptiness in their Buddhist context.

readingPath.title: Read with commentary
readingPath.note: Choose a teacher or scholar who explains the tradition explicitly.

keyInsights: The whole text provides context for its best-known lines.
Short scripture can require substantial conceptual background.
Philosophical parallels do not establish scientific equivalence.

sources.title: 84000: The Heart of the Perfection of Wisdom

title: Sri Guru Granth Sahib
author: Sikh Gurus and other devotional poets
summary: The Sikh scripture, revered as the living Guru, brings together devotional compositions with a deep relationship to music and communal practice.
context: Its status in Sikh life exceeds that of a philosophical anthology. Read with awareness of worship, service, and the community that preserves it.
editionNote: Use an identified Gurmukhi text and named English translation. Musical organization and terminology deserve explanation from Sikh sources.

readingPath.title: Sikh orientation
readingPath.note: Begin with an introduction to the scripture’s role as Guru.

readingPath.title: Japji Sahib
readingPath.note: Study the opening composition with Sikh commentary.

readingPath.title: Listen with context
readingPath.note: Explore the relation between the written compositions and kirtan.

keyInsights: The scripture includes multiple devotional voices.
Music is part of its organization and reception.
Translation alone does not reproduce its communal or liturgical life.

title: The Yoga Sutras
author: Attributed to Patanjali
summary: A compact classical account of yoga concerned with mind, practice, and liberation. Its scope extends well beyond physical postures.
context: Read classical Yoga on its own philosophical terms. Later yoga movements and modern wellness practices draw on it selectively.
editionNote: Edwin F. Bryant’s translation and commentary offers a substantial study edition. Distinguish the sutra from the commentary surrounding it.

readingPath.title: An orientation to the system
readingPath.note: Use the introduction to understand the philosophical vocabulary.

readingPath.title: Practice and the eight limbs
readingPath.note: Study the ethical and contemplative framework together.

readingPath.title: A slow complete reading
readingPath.note: Return to difficult aphorisms after reading their commentaries.

keyInsights: Aphorisms assume a context that commentary makes visible.
Ethical discipline belongs to the system of practice.
Modern uses of the word yoga do not all describe the same tradition.

title: Zhuangzi
author: Zhuangzi and later contributors
summary: A Daoist philosophical collection that uses stories, humour, paradox, and shifting perspectives to unsettle rigid judgments.
context: The work has a complex textual history. Its stories invite interpretation; a single neat doctrine rarely captures their full effect.
editionNote: Burton Watson’s complete translation differs in scope from editions of the Inner Chapters only. Check which chapters an edition contains.

readingPath.title: Inner Chapters
readingPath.note: Begin with the first seven chapters as a coherent starting selection.

readingPath.title: Read the stories twice
readingPath.note: Notice how a second perspective changes the apparent lesson.

readingPath.title: Explore the wider collection
readingPath.note: Use notes to understand differences across textual layers.

keyInsights: Perspective can change what looks useful or useless.
Parable and humour do philosophical work.
A complete-work edition and a selected edition serve different reading goals.

sources.title: Columbia University Press: The Complete Works of Zhuangzi

title: Vijñāna-bhairava-tantra
author: Anonymous; Shaiva Tantric tradition
summary: A historical Shaiva Tantric dialogue presenting 112 contemplative practices within a religious understanding of awareness.
context: Tantra names multiple traditions, not a single book or a synonym for sexuality. This text belongs to a particular Shaiva context.
editionNote: Christopher Wallis’s translation and introductory study identify the text and its setting. Keep modern adaptations distinct from a source translation.

readingPath.title: Historical introduction
readingPath.note: Locate the text in Shaiva Tantra before reading techniques.

readingPath.title: The framing dialogue
readingPath.note: Read the opening exchange before the individual contemplations.

readingPath.title: Study selected passages
readingPath.note: Use commentary to clarify terms; this guide is a reading map, not initiation.

keyInsights: The dialogue frames the practices within a religious worldview.
Translation choices shape how contemplative instructions are understood.
The text represents one strand within a much broader Tantric history.

sources.title: Christopher Wallis: introduction and verse one

title: Tantra Illuminated
author: Christopher D. Wallis
summary: A modern introduction to the history and philosophy of Tantric traditions, useful for placing popular uses of the word Tantra in context.
context: Wallis writes as a scholar-practitioner. The book is a modern study, not an ancient scripture or the voice of every Tantric lineage.
editionNote: Check the edition. Read alongside a named primary text to distinguish historical explanation from the source being explained.

readingPath.title: Historical map
readingPath.note: Begin with the account of traditions and lineages.

readingPath.title: Key philosophical terms
readingPath.note: Keep a short glossary in the author’s terms.

readingPath.title: Pair a primary text
readingPath.note: Read the Vijñāna-bhairava-tantra with that context in view.

keyInsights: History clarifies differences obscured by modern marketing.
A scholar-practitioner’s perspective should remain attributed.
Primary text and modern explanation serve complementary roles.

title: Autobiography of a Yogi
author: Paramahansa Yogananda
summary: Yogananda’s account of his life, teachers, and spiritual search connects personal narrative with his presentation of yoga to a wider readership.
context: First published in 1946, the book includes miraculous events as religious testimony. Those narratives do not independently establish scientific claims.
editionNote: The Self-Realization Fellowship edition represents its maintained publishing tradition. Earlier editions differ, so identify the edition when citing.

readingPath.title: Childhood and search
readingPath.note: Follow the narrative before extracting teachings.

readingPath.title: Teachers and lineage
readingPath.note: Notice how relationships shape the account of practice.

readingPath.title: Reflect on the genre
readingPath.note: Separate the author’s testimony, teachings, and your interpretation.

keyInsights: Spiritual autobiography joins remembered life with religious meaning.
Teacher-student relationships organize much of the narrative.
Personal testimony should remain visibly attributed.

sources.title: Self-Realization Fellowship: Autobiography of a Yogi

title: The Untethered Soul
author: Michael A. Singer
summary: Singer invites readers to notice the inner voice and examine their relationship with thoughts, emotions, and resistance.
context: This is a contemporary spiritual teaching. Its account of consciousness and energy belongs to Singer’s framework rather than an established scientific model.
editionNote: Begin with the original book before its sequels. Keep the language of the witness tied to the author’s interpretation.

readingPath.title: The inner voice
readingPath.note: Notice the distinction Singer draws between thought and awareness.

readingPath.title: Resistance
readingPath.note: Read his account of holding on and letting go.

readingPath.title: A daily observation
readingPath.note: Use one ordinary frustration to examine your response without forcing an outcome.

keyInsights: Thought can be noticed without immediately being obeyed.
Singer places inner resistance at the centre of his teaching.
Acceptance does not remove practical responsibility or personal boundaries.

sources.title: Michael A. Singer: The Untethered Soul

title: The Surrender Experiment
author: Michael A. Singer
summary: Singer’s memoir describes how his practice of surrender developed through everyday decisions, community, and business life.
context: Read the outcomes as one person’s account. A successful life story does not demonstrate that adopting the same philosophy guarantees similar results.
editionNote: This is the autobiographical companion to The Untethered Soul. The shift in genre matters: narrative examples are not universal rules.

readingPath.title: The early decisions
readingPath.note: Notice what Singer means by surrender in specific situations.

readingPath.title: Community and business
readingPath.note: Track where reflection meets practical responsibility.

readingPath.title: Compare the teaching
readingPath.note: Return to The Untethered Soul to separate the framework from its illustration.

keyInsights: Memoir supplies examples rather than controlled evidence.
Surrender in the story still involves action and decisions.
Your interpretation can differ from the narrator’s account of causation.

sources.title: Michael A. Singer: The Surrender Experiment

title: Living Untethered
author: Michael A. Singer
summary: A continuation of Singer’s teaching on awareness, emotional patterns, and the work of releasing inner resistance.
context: The spiritual framework is experiential. Read its claims about energy and consciousness as Singer’s account, not as clinical explanation.
editionNote: The 2022 book’s subtitle is Beyond the Human Predicament. It follows The Untethered Soul, which provides a useful orientation.

readingPath.title: Awareness
readingPath.note: Identify the perspective from which Singer asks you to observe experience.

readingPath.title: Stored reactions
readingPath.note: Read his explanation of recurring resistance.

readingPath.title: Ordinary practice
readingPath.note: Reflect on a manageable daily reaction and preserve space for deliberate action.

keyInsights: Singer moves from an account of awareness toward everyday practice.
Observation and action can coexist.
Spiritual language should not be mistaken for a medical diagnosis.

title: Wisdom Untethered
author: Michael A. Singer
summary: The Time for Questions brings Singer’s teaching into a question-led format concerned with applying spiritual ideas to ordinary life.
context: Published in March 2026. This entry is a source-based orientation to the book, not a claim of a completed personal reading or a chapter-by-chapter review.
editionNote: Use the publisher’s edition record and the author’s introduction. Readers new to Singer may prefer to begin with The Untethered Soul.

readingPath.title: Choose a question
readingPath.note: Start with the life question closest to your current concern.

readingPath.title: Trace the framework
readingPath.note: Connect the answer to Singer’s recurring account of awareness and resistance.

readingPath.title: Compare earlier books
readingPath.note: Use the original work for the underlying vocabulary.

keyInsights: The question format gives the teaching a different entry point.
Application requires judgment about your own circumstances.
A publisher’s description establishes scope, not the truth of every claim.

title: The Power of Now
author: Eckhart Tolle
summary: Tolle’s teaching on presence examines identification with thought and the tendency to live through remembered pasts and imagined futures.
context: Its metaphysical account belongs to Tolle’s spiritual framework. Read it as a perspective to examine, without treating every concept as a scientific category.
editionNote: Start with the original book and distinguish its teaching from quotations circulating online.

readingPath.title: Presence
readingPath.note: Track the distinction between immediate experience and thought about it.

readingPath.title: Identification
readingPath.note: Notice the language Tolle uses for the relationship to mind.

readingPath.title: Compare a Buddhist voice
readingPath.note: Read Thich Nhat Hanh alongside Tolle to hear differences in context.

keyInsights: The teaching centres attention on present experience.
Practical planning and contemplative presence need not be opposites.
Shared vocabulary across teachers can conceal different philosophies.

title: A New Earth
author: Eckhart Tolle
summary: Tolle extends his account of presence into a discussion of ego, identity, and human relationships.
context: Read his account of ego as the vocabulary of a spiritual teacher, rather than a replacement for psychological models.
editionNote: This is a separate work from The Power of Now. Compare how its social emphasis changes the earlier teaching.

readingPath.title: Identity
readingPath.note: Follow the ways Tolle describes attachment to roles and stories.

readingPath.title: Relationships
readingPath.note: Consider the consequences of that account for ordinary interaction.

readingPath.title: Return to presence
readingPath.note: Compare the book’s argument with The Power of Now.

keyInsights: Identity and awareness have distinct roles in Tolle’s account.
A useful concept still requires careful application.
An expansive social vision is a proposition to consider.

title: Be Here Now
author: Ram Dass
summary: An illustrated meeting of spiritual autobiography and practice, shaped by Ram Dass’s transformation and encounter with Indian devotional traditions.
context: The book belongs to a particular cross-cultural moment. Its devotional language and visual form are part of the reading experience.
editionNote: The Lama Foundation is the original publisher. Choose an edition that preserves the illustrated central section.

readingPath.title: The personal story
readingPath.note: Begin with the narrative that frames the teaching.

readingPath.title: The illustrated section
readingPath.note: Read at its own visual pace.

readingPath.title: The practice material
readingPath.note: Distinguish suggested disciplines from the memoir and imagery.

keyInsights: Form and content are closely linked in this book.
Devotion gives presence a different emphasis from secular mindfulness.
Personal transformation is narrated from a particular perspective.

title: The Miracle of Mindfulness
author: Thich Nhat Hanh
summary: A Buddhist introduction to bringing attention into ordinary activities, with a gentle emphasis on everyday practice.
context: Mindfulness here sits within Thich Nhat Hanh’s Buddhist teaching. Preserve that context when borrowing its language for work or self-development.
editionNote: Consult the Plum Village or Parallax edition record. Read the practices in context instead of treating isolated instructions as a productivity technique.

readingPath.title: Everyday attention
readingPath.note: Read the examples of attention within ordinary tasks.

readingPath.title: Practice and attitude
readingPath.note: Notice how care changes the quality of an action.

readingPath.title: Buddhist context
readingPath.note: Pair the book with an introductory primary text such as the Dhammapada.

keyInsights: Ordinary activities can become occasions for attention.
The manner of practice matters alongside the activity.
Mindfulness has an ethical and religious context here.

sources.title: Plum Village: The Miracle of Mindfulness

title: When Things Fall Apart
author: Pema Chödrön
summary: Contemplative reflections on meeting uncertainty and difficulty, grounded in Pema Chödrön’s Buddhist teaching.
context: The book offers a spiritual approach to experience. It does not promise that suffering disappears when a reader adopts the right attitude.
editionNote: Use a named Shambhala edition. Keep its Buddhist vocabulary visible when comparing it with contemporary self-help.

readingPath.title: Uncertainty
readingPath.note: Notice the invitation to stay present without demanding an immediate resolution.

readingPath.title: Compassion
readingPath.note: Read the treatment of difficulty alongside care for self and others.

readingPath.title: A considered comparison
readingPath.note: Pair with Singer and identify where their teachings diverge.

keyInsights: Uncertainty can be examined without forcing a reassuring story.
Compassion accompanies the discussion of difficulty.
Acceptance leaves room for practical care and change.

title: The Analects
author: Sayings of Confucius, compiled by followers
summary: A collection of conversations and sayings concerned with ethical cultivation, learning, relationships, and government.
context: The collection transmits Confucius’s teaching through followers. Its authority is ethical and cultural; it is not a revealed scripture or a manuscript authored by Confucius.
editionNote: David Hinton’s complete translation provides one entry point. Compare interpretations of ren and li rather than assuming one English word exhausts them.

readingPath.title: Learning
readingPath.note: Follow the recurring discussion of study and character.

readingPath.title: Relationships
readingPath.note: Read ethics within the roles and responsibilities described.

readingPath.title: Government
readingPath.note: Compare political advice with the account of personal cultivation.

keyInsights: Learning is connected with the formation of character.
Relationships give ethical concepts their setting.
Translation choices shape the understanding of central terms.

sources.title: Pan Macmillan: The Analects, David Hinton

title: Tattvartha Sutra: That Which Is
author: Umasvati
summary: A systematic Jain work concerned with reality, the soul, karma, and liberation, available in English as That Which Is.
context: This sutra is a foundational doctrinal text, not the entirety of Jain scripture. Jain traditions and commentaries should remain distinguishable.
editionNote: Nathmal Tatia’s translation, sponsored by the Institute of Jainology, offers a named study edition.

readingPath.title: The introductory framework
readingPath.note: Orient yourself to the text’s account of knowledge and liberation.

readingPath.title: Its categories of reality
readingPath.note: Build a glossary before drawing comparisons with other traditions.

readingPath.title: Ethics and liberation
readingPath.note: Read conduct as part of the larger doctrinal system.

keyInsights: A systematic text depends on its definitions.
Jain karma and liberation have their own conceptual context.
Comparison works best after understanding the text’s own terms.

sources.title: Yale University Press: That Which Is

title: Avesta: Selected Texts
author: Multiple Zoroastrian textual traditions
summary: An entry into a Zoroastrian scriptural and liturgical corpus, beginning with selected Yasna material and the Gathas.
context: The Avesta is not one authored book. The Gathas belong within the Yasna; later Middle Persian literature forms another body of sources.
editionNote: Avesta.org hosts legacy translations with different provenances. Identify the section and translator; use SOAS’s Multimedia Yasna for ritual and manuscript context.

readingPath.title: A corpus orientation
readingPath.note: Distinguish the Avesta from later Middle Persian writings.

readingPath.title: Yasna and Gathas
readingPath.note: Read selected passages with their place in the larger liturgy identified.

readingPath.title: Ritual context
readingPath.note: Consult the Multimedia Yasna project alongside the English text.

keyInsights: Liturgy and textual interpretation belong together.
Corpus, section, and translation are different levels of identification.
Historical translation archives are useful without being definitive editions.

sources.title: SOAS: Multimedia Yasna
sources.note: Academic context for manuscript and ritual study.

title: The Kitáb-i-Aqdas
author: Bahá’u’lláh
summary: Bahá’u’lláh’s book of laws, read within the Bahá’í Faith alongside supplementary texts, questions and answers, and explanatory notes.
context: Religious prescriptions have a specific community and interpretive setting. A cross-tradition reading guide should preserve that context.
editionNote: The Bahá’í Reference Library publishes the authorized English translation. Distinguish the main text from its supplementary material and notes.

readingPath.title: The introduction
readingPath.note: Begin with the authorized edition’s account of the work.

readingPath.title: The main text
readingPath.note: Follow its religious and ethical address.

readingPath.title: Questions and notes
readingPath.note: Use the accompanying material to understand interpretation and application.

keyInsights: An authorized edition makes its interpretive layers visible.
Religious law should be read in the context of its faith.
Supplementary writings can explain without becoming identical to the main text.
